files.content:
# Improved Codex: Job-Ready Software Engineering Track

This is an **addition** to the existing 263-project curriculum. The original
tracks teach concepts extremely well; this track teaches you to combine those
concepts into work that resembles a professional software project.

The goal is not to finish more tutorials. The goal is to produce evidence that
you can:

- turn an unclear request into testable requirements;
- make safe changes in an existing codebase;
- design and evolve an API and database;
- test behavior at the right level;
- ship through continuous integration;
- diagnose failures using logs and metrics;
- explain technical decisions and tradeoffs;
- collaborate through issues, commits, reviews, and documentation.

## How this track is different

| Existing curriculum | Improved Codex addition |
|---|---|
| Many focused concept exercises | One evolving, production-shaped system |
| Reference implementation is available | You implement from acceptance criteria |
| Mostly code correctness | Code, delivery, operations, and communication |
| Tests prove individual lessons | A testing pyramid protects real user journeys |
| Read and compare | Plan, implement, review, deploy, and explain |

There are no worked solutions in this folder. Hints explain constraints, not
the implementation. Keep your decisions in commits and architecture records;
that history is part of the deliverable.

## The capstone

Build **RelayBoard**, a collaborative work board for small teams:

- React + TypeScript client;
- ASP.NET Core API;
- PostgreSQL persistence and migrations;
- authentication and resource-level authorization;
- optimistic updates and real-time notifications;
- automated unit, integration, and browser tests;
- structured logging, health checks, and operational runbooks;
- containerized local development and a deployed environment.

Read [the capstone brief](capstone/README.md) before starting. You may substitute
a product domain you care about, but retain the engineering requirements.

## Recommended order

1. Complete [the starting diagnostic](START-HERE-DIAGNOSTIC.md), then record the
   baseline in [SKILLS-MATRIX.md](SKILLS-MATRIX.md).
2. Choose a session route with [LEARNING-MODES.md](LEARNING-MODES.md) and adapt
   pacing with [ACCESSIBILITY-AND-PACING.md](ACCESSIBILITY-AND-PACING.md).
3. Follow the twelve-week sequence in [CURRICULUM.md](CURRICULUM.md).
4. Use the [36-problem learning paths](CURRICULUM-LEARNING-PATHS.md) to vary
   how you enter and transfer every weekly exercise.
5. Mix in [48 micro-drills](MICRO-DRILLS.md) and no-notes practice from the
   [retrieval question bank](RETRIEVAL-QUESTION-BANK.md).
6. Use the [lab learning paths](labs/LEARNING-PATHS.md) when their week begins.
7. Use the [capstone learning paths](capstone/LEARNING-PATHS.md) to adapt each
   milestone without lowering its completion standard.
8. Score work with the [feedback and mastery rubric](FEEDBACK-AND-MASTERY-RUBRIC.md),
   and use the [study-group and mentor guide](STUDY-GROUP-AND-MENTOR-GUIDE.md)
   when another learner or reviewer is available.
9. Update [PROGRESS.md](PROGRESS.md) every week with links to evidence.
10. Finish with the portfolio case study in `capstone/CASE-STUDY.md`.

## Learn in more than one way

This track supports map-first, example-first, rule-first, test-first,
teach-back, written, collaborative, and error-driven approaches. These are
temporary modes, not fixed labels. Choose the mode that helps you enter the
topic, then rotate to a mode that exercises your weakest dimension.

Every route converges on the same evidence:

- retrieve the idea without notes;
- predict behavior before running code;
- implement and debug it;
- explain a tradeoff and failure case;
- reproduce the result after a delay.

Start a work block with [the session plan](templates/SESSION-PLAN.md). Use the
[concept-map template](templates/CONCEPT-MAP.md),
[teach-back template](templates/TEACH-BACK.md), or
[pairing template](templates/PAIRING-SESSION.md) when that mode fits the gap.

## Pick a resource by need

| Need right now | Use |
|---|---|
| I do not know where to begin | [Starting diagnostic](START-HERE-DIAGNOSTIC.md) |
| I need a different way into the topic | [Flexible learning modes](LEARNING-MODES.md) |
| I have only 10–20 minutes | [Micro-drills](MICRO-DRILLS.md) |
| I want to check retention | [Retrieval question bank](RETRIEVAL-QUESTION-BANK.md) |
| I need objective feedback | [Mastery rubric](FEEDBACK-AND-MASTERY-RUBRIC.md) |
| Attention, format, or schedule is a barrier | [Accessibility and pacing](ACCESSIBILITY-AND-PACING.md) |
| I have a peer, group, or mentor | [Collaboration guide](STUDY-GROUP-AND-MENTOR-GUIDE.md) |
| I keep repeating the same mistake | [Error-log template](templates/ERROR-LOG.md) |
| I need a weekly process review | [Learning retrospective](templates/WEEKLY-LEARNING-RETROSPECTIVE.md) |

## Tenfold expansion

After the core path—or whenever the diagnostic reveals a specific gap—open the
[tenfold training expansion](expanded/README.md). It adds:

- ten deep skill packs with 240 guided, independent, debugging, and transfer
  challenges;
- a [ten-lens matrix](expanded/TEN-X-CHALLENGE-MATRIX.md) that transforms the 48
  micro-drills into 480 distinct boundary, failure, concurrency, security,
  scale, observability, compatibility, accessibility, review, and interview
  variants;
- a [thirty-project ladder](expanded/PROJECT-LADDER.md);
- [twenty interview circuits](expanded/INTERVIEW-CIRCUITS.md);
- a [180-session adaptive plan](expanded/180-SESSION-PLAN.md).

Use the expansion selectively. More completed pages are not the goal; stronger
delayed performance and better engineering evidence are.

## Ten cards for every file

The [spaced-repetition trainer](spaced-repetition/README.md) automatically
creates ten contextual learning cards for every file in this track—including
documents, implementations, checks, configuration, and API contracts. With the
current 71 source files, that produces 710 cards; future files are discovered
automatically.

```powershell
cd improvedcodex
npm run study -- coverage
npm run study -- due 3
```

The ten cards require purpose recall, no-notes reconstruction, structure
mapping, examples and counterexamples, implementation, debugging, review,
teach-back, changed-constraint transfer, and delayed synthesis. Successful
reviews widen through approximately 2, 7, 30, 90, 180, and 365 days.

Read [the ten-card method](spaced-repetition/TEN-CARD-METHOD.md) for answer
depth and [the scheduling guide](spaced-repetition/SCHEDULING-GUIDE.md) for
daily, weekly, lapse, and workload routines.

## Executable labs

The labs begin as intentionally failing exercises, but their checks stay
skipped until you remove the `TODO` marker from the implementation.

```powershell
cd improvedcodex
npm test
```

Work on one lab at a time:

```powershell
node --test labs/01-idempotency/idempotency.check.mjs
node --test labs/02-cursor-pagination/pagination.check.mjs
node --test labs/03-structured-logging/logger.check.mjs
```

Each lab also has a `DEEP-DIVE.md`. It explains the problem twice: first with
an everyday mental model, then as an engineering state/data-flow problem. It
also explains why every acceptance check exists without supplying the final
implementation.

Each lab now also has a `PRACTICE-GUIDE.md`, which explains the problem again
through investigations, trace tables, progressive hints, extension problems,
and teach-back prompts. The curriculum and capstone follow the same layered
pattern through `CURRICULUM-PRACTICE.md` and `capstone/REVIEW-DRILLS.md`.

The shared [lab learning paths](labs/LEARNING-PATHS.md) provide a different
entry route for every lab while preserving the same acceptance checks.

Do not merely make the examples pass. In each lab README, complete the design
questions and explain what would change in a distributed production system.

## Definition of job-ready

This track is complete when another developer can clone your capstone and:

1. understand the problem in five minutes;
2. start the stack with one documented command;
3. run all checks with one documented command;
4. inspect a meaningful commit and pull-request history;
5. trace one request across the client, API, database, and logs;
6. see how failures are handled and recovered;
7. open a live demo or watch a short recorded walkthrough;
8. ask you why the system is designed this way and receive a clear answer.

Completion is evidence-based. “I read it” is not evidence; a passing test,
deployed URL, measured result, review, diagram, or written decision is.
